common_name: Prok American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Ohio Persimmon Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained to average soil; Prok is a heavy-bearing, large-fruited American persimmon selection from Ohio and typically sets a good crop of seedless fruit without a male pollinator (parthenocarpy), though a pollinator can improve fruit set and size further; cold-hardy to about -15°F, adapted to zones 5–9.

directions: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun; grafted trees first fruit in 3–5 years and are drought-tolerant once established, tolerating poor or clay soils that would stress most fruit trees. Prok is one of the most widely planted named American persimmon cultivars among permaculture and food-forest growers, selected in Ohio for its unusually large fruit — commonly 2–3 inches across, well above the size of typical wild-type American persimmon — combined with heavy, reliable production. The orange fruit ripens in mid-to-late fall and, like other American persimmons, must fully soften after frost before it loses its astringency and becomes sweet, rich, and honeyed with notes of dried apricot and date. Because the tree tends to set seedless fruit on its own, it is a practical choice where only one persimmon tree can be planted, though nearby male trees or other female cultivars can still improve yields. A vigorous, productive, cold-hardy selection well suited to zone 5–9 food forests and homestead orchards.
sources: Kentucky State University — American Persimmon Cultivar Trials

common_name: John Rick American Persimmon (Large Sweet Indiana Persimmon Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained to average soil; John Rick is a female cultivar and produces seeded fruit when a male American persimmon or compatible pollinator is within range — pair with a known male seedling or another cultivar for reliable seed-set and fruiting. Cold-hardy to about -15°F, adapted to zones 5–9.

directions: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun, ideally with a male American persimmon seedling or another pollinator cultivar nearby to ensure reliable fruit set; drought-tolerant once established. John Rick is a long-cultivated named American persimmon selection out of the Midwest, valued among heirloom fruit-tree collectors and permaculture growers for its large, richly flavored fruit and dependable productivity once a pollinator is present. The fruit ripens in fall and, as with all American persimmons, needs a hard frost or full ripening on the tree to shed its astringency, after which the deep orange flesh turns intensely sweet, custardy, and rich with notes of caramel and dried fruit. It is commonly grafted onto native persimmon rootstock and grown alongside other named cultivars in mixed persimmon plantings to guarantee cross-pollination and a heavier crop. A good choice for zone 5–9 growers assembling a diverse American persimmon collection.
sources: Kentucky State University — American Persimmon Cultivar Trials

common_name: Morris Burton American Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Seedless Indiana Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained to average soil; Morris Burton is an Indiana-origin American persimmon selection noted for good cold hardiness and reliable production of seedless fruit without a male pollinator. Adapted to zones 5–9.

directions: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and undemanding of fertile soil. Morris Burton is a named American persimmon cultivar out of Indiana grown for its combination of dependable cold hardiness, early bearing age, and consistent production of medium, seedless orange fruit without requiring a nearby male tree. The fruit ripens in mid-fall and, like other American persimmons, must fully soften on the tree or after a hard frost to lose its raw astringency, at which point the flesh turns sweet, thick, and richly flavored — excellent fresh, or processed into persimmon pudding, bread, and butter. Its good cold tolerance and self-fruiting habit make it a popular choice for northern-edge persimmon growers and for gardeners who want a single reliable tree without pollination logistics, in zone 5–9.
sources: Kentucky State University — American Persimmon Cultivar Trials

common_name: McMillan Pecan (Highly Scab-Resistant Native-Type Gulf South Pecan)

planting.note: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter while dormant, in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; McMillan is a Type II (protogynous) native-type pecan and needs a Type I pollinator such as Kanza, Elliott, or Oconee within about 150 feet for a full crop. Its exceptional scab resistance makes it especially valuable for low-spray or organic Gulf South orchards, where humidity makes pecan scab the primary disease pressure.

directions: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually to prevent rosette symptoms common in Gulf South pecan production. McMillan is a native-type pecan selection out of Mississippi long favored by Gulf South growers for its outstanding, near-immune resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum) — the single most damaging disease of pecans in the humid Southeast — which allows it to produce consistent, high-quality crops with little or no fungicide input, unlike scab-susceptible standards such as Desirable and Stuart. The nuts are smaller than many commercial cultivars, in keeping with its native-type parentage, but the kernel quality and flavor are excellent, and the tree bears reliably and precociously. Because of its disease resistance, McMillan is frequently recommended for backyard, homestead, and low-input orchard plantings across the Gulf South where fungicide spraying is impractical, and it pairs well with a Type I pollinator for full production. Zone 7–9.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Pecan Variety Recommendations for Louisiana

planting.note: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter while dormant, in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Lakota is a Type II pecan and needs a Type I pollinator such as Kanza, Pawnee, or Elliott within about 150 feet for reliable fertilization and a full crop.

directions: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually and prune to maintain an open canopy for airflow and scab management. Lakota Pecan was released through the USDA Agricultural Research Service pecan breeding program as a scab-resistant alternative to older, disease-prone standards, combining good resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum) with a large, attractive, thin-shelled nut and high kernel percentage that appeals to growers who want commercial-quality size without the heavy fungicide program that susceptible varieties demand in humid regions. The tree bears at a moderate age and produces consistent, mid-season crops of good-quality nuts well suited to both fresh eating and baking. Its disease resistance and nut size make it a strong choice for Gulf South and Midsouth home orchards and small commercial plantings seeking reduced-spray management, in zone 6–9.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Lakota pecan release notes
